title: Building a Community History of Munda Villages in Odisha
author: Mundari Samaj Editorial Desk
excerpt: The history of a community is not found only in books or government reports. It is also preserved in village names, family memories, songs, local documents, places of gathering and the knowledge…

body.text: Introduction

The history of a community is not found only in books or government reports. It is also preserved in village names, family memories, songs, local documents, places of gathering and the knowledge of elders. For Munda communities in Odisha, village-level documentation can help fill gaps in the historical record.
Mundari Samaj should build this archive with community participation and clear consent. This article sets out a responsible method; it does not claim that field interviews have already taken place.
1. Why village histories matter

General histories often describe broad regions and major political events. They may not explain how a particular village was founded, how families relate to one another, how local language use has changed or how people remember important events.
Village histories can preserve:
• local settlement memories;
• family and clan histories, where contributors wish to share them;
• changes in agriculture and livelihood;
• school and education histories;
• migration and return migration;
• local festivals and songs;
• community organisations;
• changes in language use;
• photographs and documents.
2. Preparing before an interview

Researchers should explain the purpose of the project before recording anyone. Participation must be voluntary. A contributor should be able to refuse a question, stop an interview or request that some material not be published.
Before an interview, explain:
• who is conducting the project;
• where the material may appear;
• whether audio, video or photographs will be made;
• whether translations will be published;
• how the contributor will be credited;
• whether the contributor can review the transcript;
• how to request correction or withdrawal, subject to the archive's stated policy.
Consent should be recorded in a language the participant understands.
3. Suggested oral-history questions
Use open questions and allow people to tell their story in their own order.
1. What name do you and your family use for this village?
2. What stories have you heard about how the village began?
3. Which places are important in the village's history?
4. Which languages are used by different generations?
5. What changes have you seen in work, education and everyday life?
6. Which songs, stories or festivals do you want younger people to know?
7. Are there old documents or photographs the family wishes to share?
8. Is there anything in this account that should remain private?
Do not pressure contributors to provide a single origin story. Different families may remember events differently.
4. Recording and preserving the material
For every recording, store:
• archive identifier;
• interview date and place;
• interviewer;
• narrator's preferred name or anonymous label;
• language and local variety;
• consent record;
• audio or video file;
• transcript in the original language where possible;
• translation;
• summary;
• publication permission;
• review status.
Keep an unedited preservation copy separate from the edited public version. Do not alter a recording in a way that changes its meaning.
5. Handling sensitive knowledge

Some information may be sacred, private, restricted by community practice or connected to vulnerable people and places. Do not assume that everything shared in an interview is intended for public publication.

Do not publish precise coordinates of sacred sites, private family locations or sensitive natural resources without informed community approval. Do not publish personal information about living people without permission.
6. Building a village history page
A public village page may include:
• village name and approved spelling;
• district and block;
• a general location map, if appropriate;
• a short history with attributed accounts;
• languages and varieties reported by contributors;
• approved photographs;
• oral-history excerpts;
• references to public records;
• contributor acknowledgements;
• last-reviewed date.
Clearly label each statement as a documentary record, an oral account, a community interpretation or an editor's summary.
7. Review and correction

Before publication, invite the narrator or an agreed community reviewer to check the transcript and translation. Where accounts conflict, preserve the difference rather than forcing a false agreement.
The archive should provide a correction channel and keep a record of significant edits.
Conclusion

A community history archive is strongest when it is built with the people whose lives it documents. By recording oral histories carefully, respecting consent and distinguishing memory from documentary evidence, Mundari Samaj can help preserve local Munda histories for future generations.
Editorial notes
This article is a fieldwork framework, not a report of completed interviews.
Obtain informed consent before recording or publishing.
Preserve original-language audio and transcripts where permission allows.
Ask contributors to review names, spellings and translations.

title: The Ulgulan — Causes, Events and Consequences (1899–1900)
author: Mundari Samaj Editorial Desk
excerpt: The Ulgulan — the 'Great Tumult' of 1899–1900 — grew out of forty years of struggle over Munda land, and it changed the law of Chotanagpur forever.

body.text: Ulgulan — 'the Great Tumult' — is the name the Munda people give to the rising of 1899–1900. It was far more than the story of one leader. Behind it lay forty years of petitions and lawsuits over land; within it, a religious renewal that swept the Munda country; and after it, changes in law and administration that are still felt in Jharkhand today.
The land question

The Mundas' customary land system, khuntkatti, vested rights in the descendants of the families who had first cleared the forest and founded each village. Through the nineteenth century this order was broken down. Landlords brought in non-tribal farmers and contractors — thikadars — who took over village lands, demanded ever higher rents and exacted unpaid forced labour (beth-begari). These outsiders were known as dikus. By 1874 the authority of the old Munda and Oraon chiefs had been almost entirely displaced, and in some villages the original proprietors had been reduced to labourers on their own ancestral land.
The Sardari Larai: forty years of petitions

From 1858 the Munda and Oraon sardars — hereditary chiefs and headmen — waged the Sardari Larai, a struggle conducted largely within the law. Their case rested on a simple claim: the Adivasis were the first people to clear the lands of Chotanagpur, and so held an inalienable right to them. Between 1858 and 1895 they petitioned the highest levels of the colonial state, up to the Viceroy of India and even the Secretary of State in London. The petitions won almost nothing. From about 1890 the sardars turned against European missionaries and officials as well, and a September 1892 plot against contractors and missionaries came to nothing for want of organisation.
A prophet's call

That leader was Birsa Munda. In 1895 he proclaimed a divine calling, urged his people to worship one God and give up the worship of bongas (spirits), and declared the reign of Queen Victoria over: 'Abua raj ete jana, maharani raj tundu jana' — let the kingdom of the Queen be ended, and our kingdom be established. He ordered the raiyats to pay no rent. Thousands — Mundas, Oraons and Kharias — accepted his teaching; he was arrested in August 1895 and imprisoned for two years. After his release he rebuilt his following in secret, while the terrible famines of 1896–97 and 1899–1900 deepened the anger his message spoke to.
The rising

Around Christmas 1899 some 7,000 men and women gathered to herald the Ulgulan, which spread across Khunti, Tamar, Basia and Ranchi. On Christmas Eve, attacks were made on churches in the Ranchi and Singhbhum country; the missions at Murhu and Sarwada were among the main targets, though the Birsaites declared their real enemy was the British, not Christian Mundas. On 5 January 1900 two police constables were killed at Etkedih. On 7 January the rebels attacked the Khunti police station, killed a constable and burnt the houses of local shopkeepers. The government set a reward of Rs 500 on Birsa's head, and Commissioner A. Fobes, with Deputy Commissioner H. C. Streattfield, reached Khunti with a force of 150 men.
Dombari Buru

The rebels concentrated on Sail Rakab hill at Dombari Buru, near Khunti. There, on 9 January 1900, government troops fired on Birsa's followers. How many died has never been settled: official records acknowledged only small numbers, while in Munda memory the firing was a massacre in which hundreds — men, women and children — were killed, and the hill is remembered with grief. Birsa himself escaped into the Singhbhum hills.
Capture, trial and death

On 3 February 1900 Birsa was captured in the Jamkopai forest, in the Porahat country near Chakradharpur. The crackdown was sweeping: by the Deputy Commissioner's own figures, 460 tribals were made accused in fifteen criminal cases; 63 were convicted, one sentenced to death and 39 transported for life. Six prisoners, Birsa among them, died in custody during the trials. Birsa Munda died in Ranchi jail on 9 June 1900, aged twenty-four, and with him the rising ended.
What changed

The Ulgulan failed in its immediate aim — no Munda Raj was established — but it forced the colonial state to confront the land question it had ignored for forty years. In 1905 the government created the Khunti subdivision, bringing administration closer to the heartland of the revolt. In 1908 it enacted the Chotanagpur Tenancy Act, which recognised khuntkatti rights in law and prohibited the transfer of tribal land to non-tribals — a protection that remains on the statute book. In memory, Birsa lives on as Dharti Aba, the Father of the Earth, and the self-rule he proclaimed in 1899 became one of the founding inspirations of the movement that, a century later, won the state of Jharkhand.

title: Gaya Munda and the Ulgulan Movement
author: Mundari Samaj Editorial Desk
excerpt: When the police came for Gaya Munda in January 1900, his whole household fought them — an episode the colonial records themselves document, though much of his life survives only in community memory.

body.text: Among the men closest to Birsa Munda, none is remembered in Khunti with more pride than Gaya Munda of Etkedih. When the police came for him in January 1900, his whole household — wife, sons, daughters and daughters-in-law — fought them with whatever weapons they had. The stand at his house is one of the best-documented episodes of the Ulgulan, yet beyond those few days the written record of his life is thin, and much repeated about him is later retelling. This article keeps to what can be documented — and says where the record ends.
The Sardar of Etkedih

Gaya Munda was a Birsaite sardar and one of Birsa's trusted lieutenants, named in the literature alongside Manjhia Munda and Donka Munda. His home was Etkedih village — spelled Etkdih, Itkadih or Aitkedih in different records — in the Khunti country south of Ranchi. Popular accounts call him the commander of Birsa's forces, active since the Sardari days; those details rest on retelling, not contemporary documents. His standing is not in doubt: when the authorities struck back, he was among their first targets.
5 January 1900: the arrest party

On 5 January 1900 a police party was sent to Etkedih to arrest Gaya Munda. In the dry bed of the Tajna river the party was attacked by Gaya Munda and other Birsa supporters, and two constables were killed. It was the moment the Ulgulan turned from raids on churches into open confrontation with the state.
6 January: the house at Etkedih

The next day, 6 January, the Deputy Commissioner of Ranchi, H. C. Streattfield, came with a large police party and surrounded Gaya Munda's house. Inside were Gaya, his wife Maki, his sons, his daughters Thingi, Nagi and Lembu, his daughters-in-law and grandchildren. Called on to surrender, the family refused, and fought with sticks, swords, axes and bows; the Deputy Commissioner's own report, quoted in later histories, describes the women fighting with sticks and axes and credits Maki Munda with killing a policeman with a thrown axe. The house was set on fire, the family driven out, and Gaya Munda captured. A modern scholarly study, drawing on the judicial records, notes that the defence of the household by its women is 'well documented in the official records' — a striking admission from the very administration that crushed the rising.
Trial, fate and memory

Gaya Munda was tried with the other Birsaite prisoners. Accounts based on the trial records state that he was sentenced to death, and he is remembered in Khunti as having been hanged in Ranchi jail; the women of his family were sentenced to rigorous imprisonment. The official statistics of the trials, which record only one death sentence among 63 convictions, sit uneasily beside these accounts; the discrepancy remains unresolved. What is certain is that Gaya Munda never returned to Etkedih. In community memory he stands as Birsa's commander — the head of a family that, women and men together, chose to fight rather than surrender.

title: Munda Participation in Other Adivasi Movements
author: Mundari Samaj Editorial Desk
excerpt: From the Sardari Larai to the Tana Bhagats and the long movement for Jharkhand, Munda men and women repeatedly struggled alongside their Adivasi neighbours — sometimes leading, often joining.

body.text: The Ulgulan of 1899–1900 was the most famous Munda rising, but it was neither the first nor the last time Munda men and women joined a wider struggle. Again and again — in the Sardari Larai of the nineteenth century, in the Tana Bhagat movement after 1914, and in the twentieth-century movement for a Jharkhand state — Mundas acted alongside their Oraon, Ho, Santhal and Kharia neighbours. This article traces those shared movements, keeping one distinction clear throughout: who led a movement, and who joined it.
The Sardari Larai (1858–1895): the struggle of petitions

The Sardari Larai — the 'sardars' struggle' — was a forty-year agitation by Munda and Oraon chiefs and tenants against the landlords, moneylenders and contractors who were taking tribal land. Its leaders argued that the Adivasis, as the first clearers of the Chotanagpur forests, were the rightful owners of the soil. The historian Suresh Singh describes the movement in three phases: an agrarian phase of clashes over rising rents, evictions and harassment; a revivalist phase; and a political phase in which, from 1890, the sardars turned against European officials and missionaries too, believing them hand in glove with the landlords.

For most of its life the Sardari Larai was fought with petitions and lawsuits rather than weapons: between 1858 and 1895 the sardars appealed to the highest authorities in the land, including the Viceroy and the Secretary of State for India in London. It won little. When a conspiracy of September 1892 to attack contractors and missionaries collapsed for want of organisation, the sardars' following began to look for a leader who would go further — and found him in Birsa Munda, whose own father is believed to have been a Sardari sympathiser. The Ulgulan grew directly out of the Sardari Larai's unfinished business.
The Tana Bhagat movement (from 1914): an Oraon renewal that Mundas joined

In April 1914, in Chingri village in the Gumla country, a 25-year-old Oraon named Jatra Bhagat proclaimed that Dharmes — God — had appeared to him in a vision. The Oraons were to worship God alone through prayer and devotion, give up the worship of spirits, abandon animal sacrifice and liquor, and prepare for the coming Oraon Raj, of which he would be the first king. His followers, the Tana Bhagats, refused to work for the zamindars or the government. Jatra and his leading disciples were arrested, tried and imprisoned, but others carried the movement on, and it spread across the Oraon country of Chotanagpur.

This was an Oraon movement, led by Oraons — but it did not stop at the boundary of one community. Munda and Kharia families living alongside the Oraons also joined the Tana Bhagats, drawn by the same grievances over rent and forced labour, and by the promise of a purified, self-respecting faith; the anthropologist S. C. Roy recognised it as a major new religious movement as early as 1921. In the 1920s the Tana Bhagats found a wider cause: many threw in their lot with Gandhi's movement, taking part in Satyagraha, the Non-Cooperation and Civil Disobedience campaigns, and carrying their own no-rent message into the national struggle.
The road to Jharkhand

The twentieth century turned the old language of land and dignity into organised politics. In 1938 the region's scattered Adivasi organisations came together on a single platform — the body that, as the Adivasi Mahasabha, became the political centre of the Jharkhand movement. Its leading figure was a Munda: Jaipal Singh Munda of the Khunti country, Oxford-educated, who had walked away from the Indian Civil Service and captained India's hockey team to gold at the 1928 Amsterdam Olympics. Invited to preside over the Mahasabha in 1939 and honoured as Marang Gomke — 'Great Leader' — he demanded a separate province of Jharkhand, carved out of Bihar, where Adivasi land, language and custom would be protected.

The Mahasabha united leaders of the Ho, Munda, Santhal and Oraon communities, though its most famous voice was a Munda's. After independence it was reorganised as the Jharkhand Party (1949–50), and Jaipal Singh carried the Adivasi case into the Constituent Assembly itself. He died in 1970, thirty years before his goal was reached; the movement passed through many hands after him, but on 15 November 2000 — Birsa Munda's birth anniversary — Jharkhand at last became a state. A movement the sardars had begun with petitions in 1858 had, a century and a half later, redrawn the map of India.

title: The Munda Clan (Killi) System
author: Mundari Samaj Editorial Desk
excerpt: As recorded by S. C. Roy in 1912, the Munda tribe was divided into a large number of exogamous clans called kilis — brotherhoods whose members traced descent from one common ancestor, stood by one another in weal and woe, and married only outside the clan.

body.text: As recorded by S. C. Roy in The Mundas and Their Country (1912), the Munda tribe was divided into “a large number of exogamous groups called kilis”. A killi (Roy also spells it kili, and calls it a sept or clan) was a brotherhood: by tradition, all its members were descended from one common ancestor, and descent was traced through the father. This article draws on Roy's 1912 ethnography and the 1961 Census monograph of Jojohatu village. Both are historical records; clan practice today varies from family to family and place to place.
One ancestor, one brotherhood

Roy describes the members of a killi as “bound to stand by one another in weal or woe”. They shared property in common, joined in common worship, and buried their dead in a common sasan (burial ground). An injury done to any one member from outside “came to be looked upon as a common injury”, and would be resented and avenged by all. Roy adds that many stories were still told of how a killi combined, in earlier times, to punish wrongs done by outsiders to its members.
How a killi gets its name

According to Roy, distinctive killi names were coined “from some memorable incident connected with the clan”, or from some circumstance of religion or belief, and many names carry an origin story. The ancestors of the Tuti killi, crossing a swollen river in winter, sent burning charcoal across to their shivering kinsmen in a forked twig of the tuti plant; the men, relieved from the cold, vowed never to eat that plant again and formed a separate killi. The Horo or Kachua (tortoise) killi took its name from a tortoise that carried the clan's ancestor, his family and his luggage across a flooded river: “No Munda of the kili will kill a tortoise or eat its flesh.” The Nag killi honoured a white Nag serpent that, in the story Roy records, carried a dead snake-charmer's body home to his sons; no member of that killi would injure a Nag serpent. Other names Roy mentions include Bando, the wild cat, and Tan or Tau, the sparrow.
Marriage must go outside the killi

The killi was exogamous: as Roy puts it, marriages between descendants of the same common paternal ancestor were interdicted, so a spouse always had to be found in another killi. As the clans grew enormous, Roy suggests, they subdivided into separate kilis, in part so that members would not have to travel far into another clan's country “to seek wives for their sons or husbands for their daughters”. Within the wider community the boundary ran the other way: by the custom Roy records, Mundas did not marry into the other ‘Kolarian’ tribes — Santals, Kharias, Asurs or Bhumijes — with a local exception for the Bhumijes of Pargana Pitkum, adjoining Tamar, who intermarried with the Mundas of that side. The Jojohatu monograph shows the exogamy rule had teeth: it recorded a boy and a girl of the same gotra who fell in love; when the girl conceived, the villagers unanimously decided the couple should be evicted, and they left the village to the beating of drums.
The clan in village life

The killi was also a working institution. When members of one killi founded new villages, Roy records, they at first went on burying their dead in the common sasan of the parent village and joined in public worship at the parent village's Sarna; allied villages of the same killi formed a parha, which became, in his words, “the unit of social as well as political organisation”, acting as one body in social and administrative matters. The parha's Panchayat judged breaches of the marriage laws, disputes over burial rights in the sasan, inheritance and boundary disputes. Yet Roy notes that social matters could not be decided by ‘kili-hagas’, clan brethren, alone: the opinion of ‘kutumbs’ — men of other kilis, with whom alone marriage relations could be entered into — had also to be consulted. The 1961 Census monograph of Jojohatu village gives the same structure at village scale: its traditional Panchayat, it says, consisted of members of the killi and used to be convoked by the Manki and the Pahan. Jojohatu's own Mundas were mostly of the Hassa killi — though a village story said they had originally been Hansda, changing to Hassa at the time of the first Revenue Settlement to distinguish themselves from their Hansda neighbours.

Roy's account dates from 1912 and the Jojohatu monograph from 1961. They are preserved here as records of what those observers found; how far any family or village follows these clan rules today is something each community can best say for itself.

title: Traditional Munda Marriage and Social Customs — as recorded in 1912
author: Mundari Samaj Editorial Desk
excerpt: From the omen-reading that opened marriage negotiations to the Sarandi wedding day itself, this is the account of Munda marriage customs that S. C. Roy recorded in 1912 — a historical snapshot, not a picture of today's weddings.

body.text: What follows is not a description of a Munda wedding of today. It is a summary of the marriage ceremonies described by S. C. Roy in The Mundas and Their Country (1912), together with the briefer customs he recorded for divorce, remarriage and birth. Roy himself warned of local variations between parganas, and much has changed since 1912.
First, the omens: Chenre-uri

In Roy's account, matches were ordinarily arranged by the father or guardian, though in earlier times, he notes, young people had a freer choice among the marriageable kilis. When a father had a suitable bride in view for his son, he sent a go-between called a Dutam to the girl's guardian. A day was then fixed for the Chenre-uri, the omen-reading. The boy's party walked to the girl's village marking every omen on the way. Among good omens Roy lists a cow and her calf lowing in answer to each other, and pitchers of water being carried; among bad ones, a man carrying an axe or spade, and a tree falling under the woodcutter's axe. One bad omen was enough: the party turned back at once and the negotiations fell through. If the omens held, the guests were seated on mats in the courtyard, their feet washed by the women of the house, and feasted with rice-beer, boiled rice and pulse. On a return visit, a spokesman — the joarni — declared the match in a set speech before Sing Bonga and the Panch: “the boy's father and the girl's father will thatch two roofs with one bundle of straw” — the two families made one.
The betrothal (Bala) and the bride-price, gonong-taka

At the Bala or betrothal, Roy records, the bride-price was settled not by naming figures but by symbols — clay marbles for the rupees wanted, rolled sal leaves tied with coloured thread for the saris. The groom's guardian kept some tokens and returned the rest, showing how much he agreed to give. The two guardians then embraced, and the Munda or Pahan of the bride's village clasped hands with his counterpart of the bridegroom's village, each binding himself to a money fine if he broke the betrothal. The bridegroom-elect was seated on the knees of his betrothed's maternal uncle and received a new cloth and a bead necklace. Later, the bride-price, the gonong-taka, was carried to the bride's house (the Gonongtaka-Idituka), and the Logon-tol fixed the wedding day.
The wedding day: Sarandi

A few days before the wedding, a mud pulpit called a mandoa was raised in the courtyard of both houses, with sal saplings at its corners and centre. Bride and bridegroom were anointed with turmeric at their own homes (the Sasang-goso), and a drop of blood from each one's little finger dyed two small rags called sinai. At the bride's house came the Sinduri-Rakab: the couple were carried three times round the mandoa and made to stand on sal-leaf plates, she facing east and he west; he pressed the toes of her right foot with his left foot and touched her neck three times with his blood-dyed rag, and she did the same to him. They exchanged garlands of gulaichi flowers, each put three vermilion marks on the other's forehead, and their garments were knotted together. Then four unmarried girls fetched water from a tank or river, escorted by women with sword and bow and by Ghasi musicians; in the Dul-da ceremony the couple, seated on yokes beside a plantain tree, anointed each other with oil and turmeric and were bathed with that water.
Divorce, remarriage — and a note on birth

Roy also records how a marriage could be dissolved. In the Sakam-Chari divorce, a Panchayat was convened and the party unwilling to continue the marriage tore a sal leaf in two; in Pargana Tamar a piece of turmeric was broken as well (Sasang-haid). If the wife was the unwilling party, the bride-price (gonong-taka) and the tora-taka had to be returned. A widow, Roy says, could remarry only in the simpler Sagai form, without the Sarandi ceremonies: the bridegroom came with some relatives to the bride's house, the party was feasted, and he took the bride home; in some localities the couple simply put sindur marks on each other's foreheads. Roy also records birth customs: a fowl was set apart in pregnancy and rice-beer brewed for Garasi Bonga, guardian of expectant mothers; on the eighth day came the Chati purification; and at the Sakhi name-giving, grains of rice were dropped into water in the names of ancestors — the baby was named after the ancestor whose grain met the baby's grain, and that relative became the child's sakhi or mita (namesake).
This is a 1912 record of Chotanagpur practice, offered as history; today's weddings blend old and new as each family chooses.

title: Munda Folk Songs and Dance
author: Mundari Samaj Editorial Desk
excerpt: As recorded by S. C. Roy in 1912, almost every Munda religious festival had its own dance and its own songs, turning with the seasons in a regular yearly round — and in 1961 the Census monograph of Jojohatu village still found community singing and dancing the village's most sought-after entertainment.

body.text: As recorded by S. C. Roy in The Mundas and Their Country (1912), “All the distinctively Mundari religious festivals, with the single exception of the Kadleta, have each its appropriate dance and songs. ” Half a century later, the 1961 Census monograph of Jojohatu village still described participation in community singing and dancing as “the most sought-for form of entertainment during leisure hours”.
A round of dances through the year

Roy names the principal classes of Mundari songs and dances as the Mage or Jarga, the Jadur, the Japi, and the Lahsua or Karam — set in a yearly round turning with the festivals. The Mage dances and songs begin after the Sohrai festival in Kartik (October–November) and continue up to the Mage festival in December, the last fortnight being specially called Jarga. From then, the Jadur and Gena songs and dances are taken up until the Sarhul or Ba-parob festival in Chait (March–April) — one Gena being sung after every two Jadur songs. After Sarhul come the Japi or hunting songs and dances, for two or three weeks, the season of the youths' hunting excursions. Then follow the Lahsua or Karam dances and songs, which go on right up to Sohrai again. “Thus,” Roy writes, “the Mundas have a regular round of still-returning dances all the year through.”
Standing dances and stooping dances

The Mundas classified their dances by posture, Roy explains, into the Tingu Susun-ko, the standing dances, and the Ungud Susun-ko, the stooping dances. The Jadur is a running dance (Nir-Susun): the dancers stand upright and run in a circle from right to left. The Gena, moving in a circle, and the Japi, moving in a straight line, go at a more moderate speed and are standing dances proper. The Lahsua or Karam dances are stooping dances: the dancers join hands, stoop forward and form an arc of a circle, advancing and retiring in that posture. Its subdivisions are the Khemta, “very slow and graceful”, and the Bin-sari, danced from cock-crow to sunrise, more erect. Some dances, Roy notes, pantomime agricultural operations such as reaping; and it is not religious exultation alone that prompts them — “social joy and merriment also finds rhythmic expression in the steps of the dance”. There are special dances for marriage festivals too (arandi-susun), one of them named the Dom-kachi.
The akhra: the village's open-air hall

The stage for all this was the akhra. Roy describes the akhra as an open space, usually near the middle of the village, under an old wide-spreading tree — where public meetings and Panchayat sittings were held, and where “the young folk of the village assemble in moon-lit nights and on festive occasions to dance and sing”. The 1961 Census monograph of Jojohatu village found the same institution in place: the akhra an open space about thirty feet square, with raised stone slabs on one side as benches — “the place for dance-meets in which both men and women participate” and “also the venue of social gatherings in the village”. It catches the akhra's evening sound too: no sooner have the people settled after their night meals than “beats of the drum may be heard from the Akhara, and gradually people trickle to the place in groups of twos or threes”.
The instruments the records name

Roy lists the instruments of his day. The drums are the dholki, small, of wood and goat-skin; the nagera, a large iron drum with ox or buffalo hide; and the dumang, earthen-framed, with monkey-skin heads. With them go the dhanpla (tambourine) and the kartal (brass cymbals); the saranga fiddle; the tuhila, a one-stringed banjo of pumpkin gourd, and the banam, a two-stringed banjo of two gourds; and the bamboo flutes, the rutu and the smaller murli. At paiki dances, young men wore ankle-bells called ghugura. At marriage festivals, Roy says, the Mundas employed musicians of the Ghasi community, whose principal instruments were the dhink drum, the narsingha horn and the perened pipe. The Jojohatu monograph, for its part, mentions only “beats of the drum” at the akhra, without naming the instrument.
Songs on the page, and change in the air

Roy's book also prints Mundari song texts with English renderings, including Jadur love-songs. The Jojohatu monograph's Karma festival likewise ends in dance — all-night singing and dancing, and next day the dancers going from house to house, received at each with a cup of handia. Yet the monograph also caught change in 1961: Jojohatu's schoolboys, it records, were not allowed to join the dancing — though the young Munda headmaster himself was an active participant.
Both books are historical records — Roy's of 1912, the monograph's of one village in 1961 — and how each village keeps its akhra and its festival round today is for that village to describe.

title: Manki–Munda: Traditional Governance
author: Mundari Samaj Editorial Desk
excerpt: How Munda and Ho villages governed themselves for centuries — through the village Munda, the Manki of the parha, and councils bound by custom — and how that system was written into Wilkinson's Rules, tested in court, and is still discussed in Kolhan today.

body.text: Long before district offices reached Chotanagpur and Kolhan, Munda and Ho villages governed themselves. Authority was layered and local: each village had its headman, groups of villages stood under a wider chief, and councils of elders settled disputes by custom rather than written law. Beside this secular order stood a second, sacred one, led by the village priest. Together — Munda, Manki and Pahan — they formed a system of self-governance that in Kolhan survives, in adapted form, to this day.
The village: the Munda and the council of elders

S. C. Roy's The Mundas and Their Country (1912) describes each Munda village as occupied by the descendants of the family that had first cleared its land. Its headman, the Munda, was the village's secular head. He did not judge alone: a village Panch, a council of elders, arbitrated disputes with him. Custom was the recognised law; offences drew fines and, in extreme cases, expulsion from the village community. In the Ho country of Kolhan the same office exists today: one hereditary Munda per village, resolving its disputes.
The parha: the Manki, first among equals

Above the village stood the parha, or patti — a group of villages acting together. Roy describes villages grouped 'generally of twelve — but sometimes more and sometimes less', with the strongest of their headmen becoming the Manki, or patti-chief, to whom the others owed allegiance. In Kolhan the corresponding unit is the pir, generally eight to fifteen villages; a settlement record quoted in the Mora Ho judgment counted 26 pirs in the Kolhan estate. The Manki presided over the Patti-Panch or Parha-Panch, the council for disputes between villages and matters of tribal importance. Yet Roy is careful: the Manki, like the Munda, 'was always looked upon as a chief among equals — a leader and not a ruler', and no superior rights of property belonged to his office. Both offices, first filled by choice of the strongest, gradually became hereditary.
The Pahan: the village's other pillar

Village leadership had two halves. Beside the Munda, the secular head, stood the Pahan — in Roy's words, the ecclesiastical head, the village priest. The Pahan led the village's worship: the offerings to the village deities and the spirits of the place. Roy suggests that in the earliest remembered order the two functions were not yet separated, and the founder's heir was chief in temporal as well as spiritual matters. The division that followed — Munda for order, Pahan for the sacred — is still recognised in Munda villages.
1833–1837: Wilkinson's Rules and the Kolhan settlement

After the Ho and Kol risings of the early nineteenth century, the British, unable to subdue Kolhan by force alone, chose to work through its traditional leaders. Captain Thomas Wilkinson, the Company's Political Agent, drafted a set of 31 rules in 1833 as guiding principles for the Ho leaders — described as the first formal codification of any adivasi community's traditional system. When the Kolhan Government Estate was created in 1837, the rules took effect there, and a Hukuknama — a record of rights — recorded the duties of Mankis and Mundas. Recognition came at a price: leaders who had never collected revenue became intermediaries of the colonial administration, and ideas of individual property entered with them.
Custom, not statute: the Mora Ho judgment

Remarkably, Wilkinson's Rules were never formally sanctioned. In Mora Ho v. State of Bihar (2000), a Full Bench of the Patna High Court held by majority that the Rules had not been framed by the Governor-General in Council — the only authority competent under Regulation XIII of 1833, and therefore lacked statutory force. The settlement reports of Ranchi (1910) and Kolhan (1913–1918) had themselves recorded that the Rules were framed 'though not sanctioned by the Government'. Yet the Court noted the Rules had been followed in Kolhan's civil justice for about 150 years, and directed that they continue until suitable replacements were framed. In Kolhan, then, the Manki–Munda order rests on custom — on a century and a half of practice — rather than on any statute.
The system today

The Kolhan Government Estate was dissolved after Independence, but Wilkinson's Rules continued in Kolhan's civil justice, the region remaining largely exempt from general civil procedure laws. In 2021 the Jharkhand government recognised the traditional Nyaya Panch for revenue-related work such as reporting land transactions and settling disputes. That balance is still negotiated: in September 2025, Ho villagers in West Singhbhum protested over feared interference with the system; the administration responded that Mankis and Mundas remain integral to it. Within the community there is also discussion about how a hereditary system should adapt to modern administration. The system endures not as a museum piece, but as a living institution whose terms are still debated by the people it governs.

title: Mundari Dialects and Regional Differences
author: Mundari Samaj Editorial Desk
excerpt: Mundari is one language, but it is not spoken the same way everywhere. Linguists describe four main varieties — Hasada, Naguri, Tamaria and Kera — and this article explains what is known about them, and why no variety should be called the 'wrong' one.

body.text: Mundari is one language, spoken across a wide region of Jharkhand, Odisha and neighbouring states — and, like every widely spoken language, it changes from place to place. A word pronounced one way in a village near Khunti may sound different in Ranchi town or in Mayurbhanj, and grammar shifts a little too. Linguists who have documented Mundari over the past century usually describe this variation through four main named varieties. Knowing them helps us listen better — and helps this archive record each speaker's words faithfully, in the form in which they were actually spoken.
Four named varieties

The linguist Toshiki Osada, following the classification in Hoffmann's Encyclopaedia Mundarica, lists four dialects of Mundari, spoken mostly in Jharkhand. Hasada is the variety east of the Ranchi–Chaibasa road. Naguri is spoken west of the same road. Tamaria — also called Latar — belongs to the Panchpargana area: Tamar, Bundu, Rahe, Sonahatu and Silli. Kera is the variety of Ranchi city and its surroundings, spoken largely by Oraon (Kurukh) families who have made Mundari their own. The Central Institute of Indian Languages' Mundari corpus documentation names the same four — Hasada, Naguri, Tamaria and Kera — as the primary varieties of the language.
How the varieties differ

The differences are real but modest beside what the varieties share. Osada notes a difference in sounds: Naguri and Kera possess aspirated stops — sounds of the kh, th type — that Hasada and Tamaria do not have. The CIIL corpus description observes that Kera's core vocabulary is close to that of the other three varieties, but its verb formations are noticeably different, both in how new verb forms are derived and in how they are inflected. Osada's own widely used grammatical description of Mundari is based mainly on Hasada — which is one reason Hasada appears so often in books. That is a fact about where documentation happened, not a ranking of the varieties themselves.
Where scholars draw the lines differently

The boundaries of a language are not always drawn the same way. Bhumij, for example, is listed in many sources as a separate language; the linguist Gregory Anderson has suggested it may instead be a variety of the Tamaria (Latar) group. It is spoken across parts of Jharkhand and in Mayurbhanj district of Odisha. Reference works do not all place Bhumij in the same position, and classifications of Mundari's varieties can differ in detail from one scholar to another. The four-variety picture above is the most commonly cited one — but it should be read as a map drawn by linguists, not as walls between villages.
No variety is the 'wrong' Mundari

It matters to say this plainly: there is no 'incorrect' Mundari. A variety is simply the speech a community has shaped in its own place over generations — in the Panchpargana villages, in Ranchi's Oraon neighbourhoods, in the Hasada country east of the Ranchi–Chaibasa road, and in the Mundari-speaking districts of northern Odisha such as Mayurbhanj, Keonjhar and Sundargarh, where the language lives alongside Odia. Differences in pronunciation or vocabulary between these places are the normal life of a language, not errors to be corrected into somebody else's speech.
Why this archive records your variety

This is why Mundari Samaj asks contributors not only for a word, song or story, but also for where it comes from. When a word is recorded, we note the village and the variety it belongs to, and we keep the contributor's own form rather than silently rewriting it into a different variety. A dictionary or story collection that mixes varieties without labels teaches confusion; one that labels them honestly teaches the language as it truly is — one language, spoken with many local voices, all of them worth preserving.

title: Mundari Oral Literature and Proverbs
author: Mundari Samaj Editorial Desk
excerpt: For most of its history, Mundari's literature lived in memory and voice — tales, songs, riddles and proverbs taught in the evening dormitories. This article traces that tradition and the two great records that preserved parts of it in writing: Roy's book of 1912 and the Jojohatu monograph of 1961.

body.text: Before Mundari had printed books, it had something older and, for centuries, sufficient: a literature carried in memory and voice. Tales told after dark, songs for work and festival, riddles traded as a game of wit, proverbs that compressed judgement into a single line — together these formed the Munda community's library. Nothing was written down, yet very little was left unrecorded; it was recorded in people. This article looks at how it lived, what it carried, and how parts of it were written down.
The evening school: folklore in the giti-ora

S. C. Roy, whose The Mundas and Their Country (1912) remains a foundational record, put it directly: for the ordinary Munda of his time, the only vehicle of instruction and culture was folklore — kahani — consisting of narratives or folktales, riddles and proverbs. These were 'recited and learnt in the evening' by the young bachelors and maidens in their respective giti-oras, the village youth dormitories, after the day's work was over. The dormitory was at once a sleeping-house, a club and, in Roy's phrase, an educational seminary. Roy closed his book with the literature itself: his contents give folk-tales, proverbs, and a final gathering of songs running to more than thirty pages.
Tales that carry memory and teaching

The commonest class of tales, Roy records, were prose stories called kaji-kahani; he prints one, 'The Tiger and the Thief', as a sample. Other tales carry far older freight. The Asur legend, which Roy retells, remembers the Asurs, an iron-smelting people, and tells how their furnaces, worked day and night, sent up a heat that dried the streams and scorched the earth, until the creatures of the world complained to Sing Bonga, who sent bird messengers ordering the Asurs to work by day or by night, but not both. The Asurs refused, and the tale moves toward their fall. A story like this is many things at once: a memory of an earlier people and their craft, an explanation of the world, and a teaching about excess and its price. Oral tales also carried the community's law in portable form — Roy records the solemn oath formula of the Mundas, invoking 'Sing-bonga on high, and the Panch on earth', a whole theory of authority held in one remembered line.
Songs and riddles

Songs accompanied the year's round of festivals, dances and work, and Roy's collection shows they could also carry commentary on life as it was being lived — including songs of indignation at wrongs suffered. Riddles were the evening's lighter discipline: posed and solved in the giti-ora, they sharpened the young in the precise, playful use of their language — its sounds, double meanings and images drawn from fields, forests and animals. Between tale, song, riddle and proverb, a young person absorbed vocabulary, history, custom and conduct without ever opening a book.
Written down twice: 1912 and 1961

Twice in the twentieth century, recorders wrote this oral world down at length. Roy's 1912 book printed Mundari tales, riddles, proverbs and songs alongside his history of the community. Half a century later, the Census of India's village monograph on Jojohatu (1961, published 1963), by S. D. Prasad, preserved another great tale in full: the legend of Karma and Dharma, which explains the Karma festival. It tells of Karma, who in anger destroyed the Karam branches and his brother's seedlings, lost his wealth, and journeyed in search of Karam Raja, by whose grace fortune returned. The monograph sets the tale beside the festival as Jojohatu kept it — on the eleventh day of Bhado, with branches of the Bhelwa tree, song and all-night dancing, no sacrifice, and the festival observed in alternate years. Both tales are now retold on this website — 'The Asur Legend' and 'Karma and Dharma — the legend of Karam Raja' — each with its source named.
Proverbs: a shelf still being filled

A word of honesty about proverbs. Roy printed a few pages of Mundari proverbial lore as samples, remarking on how much judgement the form can carry. But a proverb is not only a sentence; it belongs to a place, a speaker and an occasion, and its force often lies in when it is said. A trustworthy collection must therefore record each proverb with its source — who used it, where, and in what variety of Mundari — rather than gathering unattributed sayings from anywhere. Such a sourced Mundari proverb collection is still being built for this archive, and we would rather leave the shelf partly empty than fill it with lines we cannot vouch for. If your family keeps proverbs, songs, riddles or tales, the Contribute page explains how to share them with place and teller recorded — so the next recorder of this literature can be the community itself.
